title: Bootstrap 5: Grid, Components, Themes
summary: Build a responsive page fast with Bootstrap 5.3: the grid, components and utilities, interactive plugins, and color modes.
intro: Bootstrap is one of the most used CSS frameworks on the web. It runs admin dashboards, internal tools, older apps, and thousands of ready-made themes, and a team that needs a clean, responsive page by Friday still reaches for it. At work, you're likely to be asked to change a page built with it, or to build one. This lesson teaches Bootstrap 5.3, the current version: how to add it to a page, its grid for laying out a page at every screen size, the components and utility classes you'll see in every Bootstrap page, the interactive parts that need its JavaScript, and how to change its look, dark mode included. By the end, you'll be able to read any Bootstrap page and build your own.

steps.title: Adding Bootstrap
steps.body:
Before anything else, Bootstrap's files have to reach the page. Both ways to add a library from the last lesson work, and the one you pick decides how easily you can trim and change Bootstrap later.

## From a CDN

The quickest start is Bootstrap's starter page (example 1): a stylesheet in the head and a script at the end of the body, both from the jsDelivr CDN, each with the `integrity` hash the last lesson explained. Copy the two tags from Bootstrap's own docs, at getbootstrap.com, which always show the current version and its hashes.

The viewport `<meta>` tag from the HTML lessons matters more than usual here. Without it, phones pretend to be wide screens, and Bootstrap's layout never switches to its phone version.

## From npm, through Vite

In a project with a build, run `npm install bootstrap` and import it from your main module (example 2). Bootstrap lists `@popperjs/core` as a **peer dependency**, a package it expects your project to have, and npm installs that for you too. Vite bundles both into your own hashed files, as the bundling lesson showed.

## The bundle, or not

Bootstrap's JavaScript comes in two versions. `bootstrap.bundle.min.js` includes **Popper**, a small library that places dropdowns, tooltips, and popovers next to the thing they belong to, and keeps them on screen near the edge of the window. `bootstrap.min.js` leaves Popper out, for pages that load it separately or use none of those three. When in doubt, use the bundle.

Older versions of Bootstrap needed jQuery as well. Version 5, from 2021, dropped it, so a page that loads jQuery only for Bootstrap 5 can take it out. When you see code like `$("#confirm").modal("show")` in a project, that's the jQuery style older versions required, and the jQuery lesson helps you read it.

## What's in the stylesheet

Bootstrap's CSS has five kinds of rules, and knowing them makes any Bootstrap page easier to read:

- **Reboot** is Bootstrap's reset. It evens out the browsers' default styles from the cascade lesson, sets `box-sizing: border-box` on everything, and picks a font that matches each computer's system.
- **Layout** is the containers and the grid, in the next part.
- **Content** styles plain HTML: headings, lists, tables, images, and form fields.
- **Components** are the named pieces: buttons, cards, navigation bars, alerts, dialogs, and dozens more.
- **Utilities** are one-job classes for spacing, display, Flexbox, colors, and text, much like Tailwind's.

Underneath all of them are custom properties whose names start with `--bs-`, which part 5 uses to change the look. The whole stylesheet is 232 kB, or 31 kB compressed.

examples.title: The starter page
examples.prompt: Bootstrap's starter page, with the version and hashes from its docs. Save it as `index.html` and open it in a browser.
examples.code: Find your next trail
examples.explanation: The stylesheet is in the head, since the page needs its styles before the first paint. The script sits at the end of the body, the classic way, so the parser reaches it last and it can't hold up the page. Both name an exact version, 5.3.9, so the file never changes under you, and both carry an `integrity` hash and `crossorigin="anonymous"`. The `<main>` uses three Bootstrap classes: `container` centers the content at a comfortable width, `py-4` adds padding above and below, and `btn btn-primary` makes a blue button. Even the heading looks different from the browser's default, because Reboot and Bootstrap's content styles change it.

examples.title: Importing Bootstrap through Vite
examples.prompt: In a Vite project, after `npm install bootstrap`, these two lines go at the top of `src/main.js`, in place of the CDN tags.
examples.explanation: The first line imports the stylesheet from the package's `dist` folder, and Vite turns it into a hashed CSS file and links it from the built page. The second imports Bootstrap's JavaScript as a module, which sets up every component that works through attributes, like the dialogs and menus in part 4. In our build, that was 81 kB of JavaScript, or 24 kB compressed. Bootstrap's components set themselves up the moment they load, so the bundler can't drop the ones you don't use. To include fewer, import each one from its own file, like `import Modal from "bootstrap/js/dist/modal"`, which came to 23 kB for the modal alone.

steps.title: The grid and breakpoints
steps.body:
Most pages need a layout that changes with the screen: one column on a phone, two on a tablet, three on a laptop. Bootstrap's grid does that with three kinds of class, and once you can read them, you can read the layout of any Bootstrap page.

## Containers, rows, and columns

- A **container** centers the content and gives it a maximum width. `.container` grows in steps as the screen widens: the full width on a phone, then 540, 720, 960, 1,140, and 1,320 pixels. `.container-fluid` is always the full width.
- A **row** holds columns, and lines them up side by side.
- A **column** is a slot in the row. A row is split into 12 equal parts, and a column's class says how many it takes: `col-6` is half, `col-4` a third, and `col-3` a quarter. A plain `col` shares the row equally with the other columns.

Why 12? It divides evenly into halves, thirds, quarters, and sixths.

## Breakpoints

A breakpoint, from the lesson on responsive CSS, is a screen width where the layout is allowed to change. Bootstrap has six:

| Name | In a class | From |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Extra small | nothing | 0 |
| Small | `sm` | 576px |
| Medium | `md` | 768px |
| Large | `lg` | 992px |
| Extra large | `xl` | 1,200px |
| Extra extra large | `xxl` | 1,400px |

The name goes in the middle of a class: `col-md-6` means half the row, from medium screens up. Like the media queries in the CSS lessons, Bootstrap is **mobile first**. A class without a breakpoint applies at every width, and one with a breakpoint applies from that width up, until a bigger one takes over. So `col-12 col-md-6 col-lg-4` reads: the full width on phones, half from 768 pixels, and a third from 992.

```diagram bootstrap-grid
The same three cards at three widths, from one set of classes.
```

In the diagram, three cards share the classes `col-12 col-md-6 col-lg-4`. On a phone, each takes all 12 parts, so they stack. From medium screens, each takes 6, two fit in a row, and the third wraps to a new line. From large screens, each takes 4, and all three fit.

## Gutters

The space between columns is the **gutter**. Each column has padding on its left and right, and the row has a matching negative margin, so the outer columns still line up with the container's edges. `g-0` to `g-5` set the gutter both ways, `gx-` only between columns side by side, and `gy-` only between rows that wrap. Example 1 uses `g-4`.

## It's Flexbox underneath

There's no magic in it. A row is a flex container from the layout lesson, with `flex-wrap: wrap`, and each column sets its own width (example 2). Columns that add up to more than 12 wrap onto a new line, which is how the cards in the diagram fall into rows. It's also why the Flexbox utilities in the next part, like `justify-content-center` and `align-items-center`, work on rows.

When every column in a row should be the same, `row-cols-*` on the row saves writing a class on each one: `row row-cols-1 row-cols-md-2 row-cols-lg-3` lays out its columns exactly like the cards in example 1.

examples.title: Three cards that rearrange themselves
examples.prompt: The starter page's `<main>`, now holding a row of trail cards. Make the browser window narrower and wider, and watch the cards move.
examples.code:
Lake Loop
Ridge Trail
North Loop
examples.explanation: The container keeps everything centered at a comfortable width, and `g-4` puts a 1.5rem gutter between the cards, both across and down. Each card sits inside a column `div`, never on the column itself, so the column's padding makes the gutter and the card's border stays clean. `h-100` makes each card the full height of its column, so cards with different amounts of text still line up. Below 768 pixels the three cards stack, from 768 two share a row and the third wraps, and from 992 all three sit in one row. The HTML never changed: only the screen did.

examples.title: The CSS behind the grid
examples.prompt: These rules are copied from Bootstrap 5.3.9's `bootstrap.css`, the version without minification. They're all the grid needs for example 1.
examples.explanation: `.row` is a flex container that wraps, and its negative margins cancel the outer columns' padding. Every child of a row starts at the full width, which is what `col-12` asks for anyway. Each column gets padding on both sides of half the gutter, so two neighbors make one whole gutter between them. The gutter itself is a custom property, `--bs-gutter-x`, and `g-4` only changes that property, so every rule that reads it follows. The `@media` rule is the breakpoint: from 768 pixels, `col-md-6` takes exactly half. `col-lg-4` is the same rule with 992 pixels and 33.33333333%. Bootstrap is built from plain CSS you already know, written once so you don't have to.

steps.title: Components and utilities
steps.body:
Most of a Bootstrap page is components with utilities added for the small adjustments. Once you see the pattern of a base class, a few modifier classes, and some utilities, any Bootstrap markup reads like a sentence.

## Components

A component is a base class that sets up the piece, plus **modifier** classes that change one thing about it:

- **Buttons:** `btn` and a color, like `btn-primary`, `btn-secondary`, or `btn-danger`, or an outlined one, like `btn-outline-primary`, and optionally a size, `btn-sm` or `btn-lg`. They work on `<button>` and on `<a>` alike.
- **Cards:** a box with a border and rounded corners. `card` makes the box, `card-body` inside it adds the padding, and `card-title`, `card-text`, `card-header`, `card-footer`, and `card-img-top` style its parts.
- **Alerts:** a colored message box, like `alert alert-warning`. Add `role="alert"` when one appears after the page has loaded, so screen readers announce it.
- **Forms:** `form-label` on labels, `form-control` on text fields, `form-select` on selects, and `form-check` around a checkbox and its label. `is-invalid` marks a field with a problem, and an `invalid-feedback` element right after it shows the message.
- **Navbar:** the bar across the top of a site, which the next part builds.

The color names, `primary`, `secondary`, `success`, `danger`, `warning`, `info`, `light`, and `dark`, are Bootstrap's **theme colors**, and they work across components: `btn-danger`, `alert-danger`, `text-danger`, and `bg-danger` all use the same red.

## Utilities

Utility classes do one job each. Bootstrap pages use them everywhere for spacing and small layout fixes, and they're marked `!important` in Bootstrap's CSS so they always win over component rules. It's one of the few places where `!important` is used on purpose.

**Spacing** classes are built from three parts, plus an optional breakpoint:

- What: `m` for margin, `p` for padding.
- Which side: `t` for top, `b` bottom, `s` start, `e` end, `x` both sides, `y` top and bottom, and nothing for all four. Start and end are the left and right in English, and Bootstrap's right-to-left version swaps them for languages like Arabic.
- How much: `0` to `5`, where 1 is 0.25rem, 2 is 0.5rem, 3 is 1rem, 4 is 1.5rem, and 5 is 3rem, plus `auto`.

So `mb-3` is a 1rem margin at the bottom, `px-4` is padding on both sides, `mt-md-5` is a big margin at the top from medium screens up, and `ms-auto` pushes something to the far end of a flex row.

The other utilities you'll see most:

- **Display:** `d-none`, `d-block`, and `d-flex`, with breakpoints too: `d-none d-md-block` hides something on phones and shows it from medium screens up.
- **Flexbox:** after `d-flex`, `justify-content-between`, `align-items-center`, `flex-column`, `flex-wrap`, and `gap-2`.
- **Text and color:** `text-center`, `fw-bold`, `small`, `text-body-secondary` for quieter text, `bg-body-tertiary` for a lightly shaded panel, and `text-bg-primary`, which sets a background color along with a text color that's readable on it.

## Reading Bootstrap markup

When you meet a long list of classes, sort it: the component first, then its modifiers, then the utilities. `class="card h-100 shadow-sm"` is a card, as tall as its column, with a small shadow. `class="btn btn-outline-secondary btn-sm ms-auto"` is a small gray outlined button, pushed to the end of its row. The docs at getbootstrap.com have a page for every component with markup to copy, and teams mostly build pages by copying it and changing the content.

examples.title: A trail card, piece by piece
examples.prompt: One card from a trail list, using components and utilities together.
examples.code:
Lake Loop

Easy

A gentle 5 km loop around the lake.

View trail
examples.explanation: `card`, `card-img-top`, `card-body`, `card-title`, `card-text`, and `card-footer` are the component and its parts, and `shadow-sm` and `h-100` adjust it. The heading is an `h2`, the right level for the page's outline, with the class `h5` to make it look smaller, which keeps meaning and looks apart as the HTML lessons asked. The top row is a flex row: `justify-content-between` pushes the title and the badge apart, `align-items-center` lines them up, and `mb-2` adds space below. `badge text-bg-success` is a small green label with readable text. In the footer, `gap-2` spaces the two buttons, and `ms-auto` pushes Save to the far right.

examples.title: A form field with an error
examples.prompt: A field the server found a problem with, the way the forms lesson said a server should send it back after a failed submit.
examples.code: Pick a date in the future.
examples.explanation: `form-label` and `form-control` give the label and the field Bootstrap's look, and `mb-3` spaces each group. `is-invalid` turns the field's border red and adds a warning icon, and it also shows the `invalid-feedback` element right after it, which Bootstrap hides until then. Bootstrap only handles the looks, so the accessible parts are yours to add, as in the forms lesson: `aria-describedby` links the message to the field so a screen reader reads it, and `aria-invalid="true"` says the value has a problem. The checkbox uses `form-check`, `form-check-input`, and `form-check-label` to line the box up with its label.

steps.title: Interactive components
steps.body:
Some components have to do something: open a dialog, drop a menu down, fold a section away. Bootstrap's JavaScript does that, and for most of it, you write no JavaScript at all, only attributes.

## Data attributes

Bootstrap's script watches the whole page for clicks on elements with a `data-bs-toggle` attribute, one of the `data-*` attributes from the HTML lessons. Its value names the component, like `modal`, `dropdown`, or `collapse`, and `data-bs-target` says which element to act on, with a CSS selector. That's the event delegation from the JavaScript lessons, one listener on the whole document, so it works for buttons added later too.

## Modal

A **modal** is Bootstrap's dialog (example 1). The button that opens it carries `data-bs-toggle="modal"` and `data-bs-target="#confirm"`, and the dialog is a `div` with the class `modal` and that id, holding a `modal-dialog`, a `modal-content`, and a header, body, and footer. Any button inside it with `data-bs-dismiss="modal"` closes it.

## Dropdown and collapse

A **dropdown** is a button with `data-bs-toggle="dropdown"` followed by a list with the class `dropdown-menu`, both inside an element with the class `dropdown`. Popper places the menu, and Bootstrap closes it on Escape or on a click anywhere else, and lets the arrow keys move through it.

**Collapse** shows and hides an element with a sliding animation: a button with `data-bs-toggle="collapse"` and `data-bs-target="#details"` opens and closes the element with that id and the class `collapse`. The menu button a navbar shows on phones is a collapse (example 2).

## Tooltips: turn them on yourself

A **tooltip** is the small label that appears over an element on hover or focus, and a **popover** is a bigger box that opens on a click. Both need Popper, and setting one up costs a little time for every element, so Bootstrap doesn't start them by itself. You mark them with `data-bs-toggle="tooltip"` and `data-bs-title`, then start each one in JavaScript (example 3).

## The JavaScript API

Each component is also a class your own code can use: `Modal`, `Dropdown`, `Collapse`, `Tooltip`, and the rest. From the CDN, they're on a global object called `bootstrap`, as in `bootstrap.Modal`. From npm, you import them. `getOrCreateInstance(element)` returns the component already attached to an element, or makes one, so you never end up with two on the same element. Then call `show()`, `hide()`, or `toggle()` on it.

Components announce what they're doing with events, named like `show.bs.modal`, `shown.bs.modal`, `hide.bs.modal`, and `hidden.bs.modal`, and the same pattern for the others. `show` fires just before the dialog opens, so calling `preventDefault()` on it stops the dialog from opening. `shown` fires once it's open and its animation has finished. Listen for them with `addEventListener`, like any event.

## What Bootstrap covers, and what it leaves to you

Bootstrap's JavaScript handles the hard behavior. The modal moves focus inside when it opens, keeps Tab inside it, closes on Escape, and gives focus back to the button that opened it, and the toggles keep `aria-expanded` up to date, so a screen reader can tell whether a menu is open. What it can't do is know your content. You still give each modal a heading and point `aria-labelledby` at it, give buttons with only an icon an `aria-label`, like the close button's `aria-label="Close"`, write `alt` text, keep your own colors readable, and put tooltips only on elements that can take focus, so keyboard users get them too. Bootstrap's own docs warn that carousels, slideshows that move by themselves, are hard for many people to use however they're built.

examples.title: A modal that confirms a delete
examples.prompt: A delete button and the dialog it opens, on a page that loads Bootstrap's bundle. No JavaScript of your own is needed.
examples.code:
Delete this trip?

Lake Loop on Saturday will be gone for good.
examples.explanation: The first button opens the dialog through its two `data-bs-` attributes. The dialog starts hidden: `aria-hidden="true"` keeps screen readers out of it, and `tabindex="-1"` lets Bootstrap move focus to it when it opens. `fade` adds the fade-in. `aria-labelledby` points at the heading, so a screen reader announces Delete this trip? as the dialog's name. The `btn-close` button draws an X, so it needs `aria-label="Close"` to have a name at all. Both Close and Keep it carry `data-bs-dismiss="modal"`. The real Delete button submits a form elsewhere on the page through its `form` attribute, so deleting still works as a plain form post.

examples.title: A navbar that folds up on phones
examples.prompt: The top bar of the trail site. Below 992 pixels its links fold away behind a menu button.
examples.code:
Trail Guide
  • Trails
  • Maps
  • My trips
examples.explanation: `navbar-expand-lg` says when the bar spreads out: from large screens up, the links sit in a row and the menu button disappears. Below that, the links live in the `collapse` element and the `navbar-toggler` button shows instead, with an icon and nothing else, so `aria-label` gives it a name. Its `data-bs-toggle="collapse"` and `data-bs-target="#main-nav"` open and close the links, and Bootstrap flips `aria-expanded` between false and true as it does. `ms-auto` pushes the links to the right. `active` and `aria-current="page"` mark the page you're on, one for the eyes and one for screen readers.

examples.title: Tooltips and the JavaScript API
examples.prompt: `src/main.js` in a Vite project that imports Bootstrap. It turns on every tooltip, and opens the delete dialog from example 1 with code.
examples.explanation: The loop finds every element marked for a tooltip, like `<button data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Saved trips">`, and starts a `Tooltip` on each one. The listener for `shown.bs.modal` runs once the dialog is fully open, and moves focus to Keep it, the safe choice, instead of the first focusable element. The last listener opens the same dialog when someone presses the Delete key in the trip list. `getOrCreateInstance` reuses the `Modal` that Bootstrap made when the button was clicked, or makes one if nobody has opened it yet, so there's never a second copy fighting the first. From a CDN, the code is the same, with `bootstrap.Modal` and `bootstrap.Tooltip` in place of the imports.

steps.title: Customizing and color modes
steps.body:
Every Bootstrap site starts out looking like every other one. Changing the colors, the fonts, and the corners is what makes a site yours, and Bootstrap gives you three ways to do it, from a few lines of CSS to rebuilding it from its source.

## CSS variables

Bootstrap's stylesheet reads custom properties whose names start with `--bs-`. The global ones are set on `:root`, like `--bs-body-font-family`, `--bs-body-bg`, and `--bs-border-radius`. Set them in your own stylesheet, linked after Bootstrap's, and everything that reads them follows.

Components have variables of their own. Every button reads `--bs-btn-bg`, `--bs-btn-color`, `--bs-btn-hover-bg`, and a dozen more, and `btn-primary` is nothing but a list of values for them. So the tidy way to make a new kind of button is a class that sets those variables (example 1), instead of fighting Bootstrap's rules with your own.

There's a catch. Bootstrap's source is written in **Sass**, a language that adds variables and functions to CSS and is turned into plain CSS at build time. When Bootstrap was built, Sass worked out every component's colors and wrote them in as plain values: `btn-primary` sets `--bs-btn-bg: #0d6efd`, not a reference to some primary color variable. Changing `--bs-primary-rgb` recolors the utilities that read it, like `text-primary` and `bg-primary`, but not the buttons. To change a theme color everywhere, you rebuild from Sass.

## Color modes

Bootstrap 5.3 comes with a dark theme. Put `data-bs-theme="dark"` on the `<html>` element and the whole page switches: backgrounds, text, borders, and every component. It works on any element, so `data-bs-theme="light"` on a single card keeps that card light inside a dark page.

Bootstrap doesn't follow the computer's light or dark setting by itself. To do that, and to offer a switch, you set the attribute with a few lines of JavaScript, using `matchMedia` and `localStorage` from the lesson on fetch and other Web APIs (example 2). Bootstrap's docs publish a longer version of the same script.

## Sass: building your own Bootstrap

Teams that customize a lot install Bootstrap and the `sass` package from npm, and write a `.scss` file that sets Sass variables, like `$primary` and `$border-radius`, before importing Bootstrap's source (example 3). Vite compiles `.scss` files by itself once `sass` is installed. Because Sass works out the colors, the hover shades, the outlines, and the focus rings all follow the new primary color.

The same file can import only the parts you use, instead of all of Bootstrap. With just the grid, buttons, and utilities, the stylesheet came to 99 kB in our build, where the whole of Bootstrap came to 225 kB.

## When Bootstrap fits

Bootstrap shines when you need a clean, consistent, responsive interface quickly and don't have a designer: admin panels, internal tools, dashboards, prototypes, and the many sites already built on it. It fits less well when a design has to look like nothing else, since you'd override more than you use, and in apps built with a component framework like React, where teams usually choose tools made for it. And on a page where every kilobyte counts, its 31 kB of CSS is a lot for a few buttons.

Many older Bootstrap pages also run jQuery, which the next lesson teaches you to read.

examples.title: A button in your own brand color
examples.prompt: A new button style in your own stylesheet, linked after Bootstrap's. Use it as `class="btn btn-brand"`.
examples.explanation: `btn` still does all the work: its rules read these variables for the background, the text, the border, and each state. `btn-brand` only supplies the values, the same way `btn-primary` does in Bootstrap's own stylesheet, so the new button gets every behavior of a real Bootstrap button, the focus ring included. You pick the hover and active shades yourself here, which is the part Sass would have worked out for you. Nothing is overridden, so there's no specificity fight and no `!important`, and Bootstrap can be upgraded later without breaking it.

examples.title: Following the system's dark mode
examples.prompt: A classic script in the `<head>`, before Bootstrap's stylesheet, so the right theme is set before the first paint. A button with the id `theme-toggle` switches it.
examples.explanation: `matchMedia` asks the same question as the CSS media feature, and its `matches` is true when the computer is set to dark. `applyTheme` uses the visitor's own choice when there is one, and the system's setting when there isn't, and writes it to `data-bs-theme` on `<html>`, which `dataset.bsTheme` names in JavaScript. Two short forms do the choosing. `a ?? b` gives `a`, or `b` when `a` is `null` or `undefined`. `a ? b : c` is an if and an else in one line: `b` when `a` is true, and `c` when it isn't. It runs at once, so the page never flashes light before going dark, and again whenever the system setting changes. The toggle's listener waits for `DOMContentLoaded`, the event the document fires once the whole page has been parsed, since this script runs in the head before the button exists. It saves the opposite theme and applies it. Reading and writing `localStorage` sit inside `try`, since some browsers refuse storage in private windows, and the page should still work there.

examples.title: Bootstrap rebuilt with your own colors
examples.prompt: `src/custom.scss` in a Vite project with `bootstrap` and `sass` installed. `src/main.js` imports it with `import "./custom.scss"`.
examples.explanation: Lines that start with `$` are Sass variables, and Bootstrap's source uses them for every decision. Setting them before the import replaces Bootstrap's defaults, so this file builds a Bootstrap whose primary color is green everywhere: buttons, links, focus rings, and the shades Sass works out for hover and active. Vite compiles it to plain CSS at build time. Bootstrap 5.3 still uses Sass's older `@import` rule, so today's Sass prints hundreds of deprecation warnings while it builds: ours said 311 repetitive deprecation warnings omitted. They're harmless, and teams hide them with `silenceDeprecations: ["import", "color-functions", "global-builtin", "if-function"]` under `css.preprocessorOptions.scss` in `vite.config.js`.

recap:
- Add Bootstrap from a CDN with pinned, hashed tags, or with npm and an import through Vite.
- bootstrap.bundle includes Popper for dropdowns, tooltips, and popovers, and Bootstrap 5 needs no jQuery.
- A container holds rows, a row holds columns, and a column takes some of 12 parts, like col-md-6.
- Breakpoints are mobile first: sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl apply from their width up.
- Components are a base class plus modifiers, and utilities like mb-3 and d-flex adjust them.
- data-bs-toggle and data-bs-target run modals, dropdowns, and collapses, but tooltips must be started in JavaScript.
- Change the look with --bs- variables, data-bs-theme for dark mode, or Sass variables in a rebuild.
